author: Niagara Action
title: Niagara Falls Threatens Foreclosure Against 3,000 Property Owners Over Unpaid Taxes - NewsBreak
text:
By Niagara Action ,
3 hours ago Thousands of property owners across Niagara Falls are now facing the possibility of foreclosure after the city issued roughly 3,000 warning letters demanding years of unpaid taxes be paid in full by the end of June.
The sweeping enforcement effort, announced by Mayor Robert Restaino’s administration, comes as city officials attempt to recover millions of dollars in delinquent property taxes that have accumulated across Niagara Falls.
According to the city, the combined unpaid balances tied to the affected properties amount to a staggering sum that the mayor himself believes represents a major threat to the city’s finances.
“The amount of outstanding property taxes is almost one-third of our total 2026 fiscal year budget so even recouping a portion of the outstanding amount due to the City would have a significant and positive impact on our budget outlook,” said Restaino.
The foreclosure notices were distributed through the city’s Billing and Collections Department and target property owners who allegedly still owe city taxes dating back to 2023.
Under the warning letters, owners are being instructed to pay all outstanding city taxes in full along with unpaid school taxes from 2024 and 2025.
City officials say there will be no extensions, no additional grace periods and no further delays.
“There is no further grace period and, if payments are not made by June 30th, the properties will be foreclosed,” said Restaino. “The City will then auction those properties through a competitive bidding process.”
The move immediately raises the stakes for thousands of Niagara Falls residents and property owners already dealing with mounting financial pressure from inflation, rising utility costs, increasing insurance rates and higher living expenses throughout Western New York.
Now, many are also facing the possibility of losing homes, rental properties or longtime family-owned buildings if balances are not fully resolved within weeks.
While city officials framed the action as financially necessary, critics of the Restaino administration are questioning how Niagara Falls allowed unpaid tax balances to spiral to levels now equaling nearly one-third of the city’s annual budget before launching such a massive foreclosure push.
The situation also highlights the broader financial strain continuing to impact Niagara Falls despite years of promises surrounding downtown redevelopment, tourism growth and economic revitalization projects.
Restaino attempted to downplay the uniqueness of the issue, arguing municipalities across New York are dealing with similar tax collection problems.
“This is a matter that is not unique to Niagara Falls as cities across the region and the state face the same dilemma of property owners who are not making property tax payments leaving municipalities with no choice but to foreclose on properties,” he said.
Still, the sheer scale of the notices – approximately 3,000 properties – signals one of the city’s largest recent foreclosure enforcement efforts.
The city has not publicly broken down how many of the affected properties are owner-occupied homes versus vacant buildings, rental units or commercial properties.
Nor has the administration detailed how many owners may already be attempting to enter repayment discussions.
Instead, the city’s position appears increasingly straightforward: pay the balances in full or risk foreclosure proceedings beginning after June 30th.
If foreclosures proceed, seized properties would eventually be auctioned through competitive bidding.
Such auctions often attract outside investors and developers searching for distressed properties at discounted prices, which is something in the past that has attracted the very people who are now probably not paying their taxes (or just contributing to blight and otherwise not caring for their properties).
The city argues recovering the unpaid taxes is essential to stabilizing municipal finances and funding services moving forward.
But for residents already stretched thin financially, the looming deadline arrives at a particularly difficult time.
Property owners receiving letters are now left scrambling to determine whether they can come up with years of unpaid taxes before the city moves to seize the properties altogether.
Officials are directing impacted residents to contact the Niagara Falls Billing and Collections Department at (716) 286-4350 for additional information regarding balances and foreclosure proceedings.
We also recommend you consult an attorney to determine whether the city would actually be able to commence a foreclosure action as easily as the Restaino administration might have you believe.

The sweeping enforcement effort, announced by Mayor Robert Restaino’s administration, comes as city officials attempt to recover millions of dollars in delinquent property taxes that have accumulated across Niagara Falls. Now, many are also facing the possibility of losing homes, rental properties or longtime family-owned buildings if balances are not fully resolved within weeks.
